rows.etymology: 173. Bng. lèkṇɔ3 v.i. ‘to jump, kick out’ and perhaps Garh. lakalyāṇ ‘to loose balance when carrying asymmetrically s.th. very broad on one’s shoulder’ (Purohit and Benjwal) or (Nautiyal and Jakhmola) ‘to move, to shake, to sway’ and lak, lak-luku ‘flexible, tender, easily bent’ may derive < PIE *lek- ‘jump, scuttle along’ as reflected e.g. in dialectal Norwegian lakka ‘to scuttle, jump on one leg’ and Latv. lekt ‘to leap, jump’. There is probably a further cognate in Garh. lekḍū ‘kamar, kūlhā – waist, loins’ (Nau- tiyal and Jakhmola), which most likely has erotic innuendoes because of semantically close H. kamar hilānā ‘to copulate’ (lit. ‘to shake the hip’) and other similar expressions with ‘hip’. There seems to be a striking parallel in Greek λεκάω which means ‘to dance to a song’ but also ‘to have intercourse’ and which Beekes derives with question mark < PIE *lek- ‘jump’. He is convinced that “. . . the meaning . . . ‘to have intercourse’ is euphemistic and secondary” (2010: 856), however, in addition, he considers relation with λαικάξω ‘to wench’ (and λαικάστρια ‘strumpet’) (ibid. and p. 823), which he interprets as possible pre-Greek words. Note: Sub Garh. lekḍū the authors write “pa(ryāy) tīg, tegḍū which they ren- der as ‘pīṭh – back’. Thus as a synonym (paryāy), pīṭh can here only have the meaning ‘stern, buttocks’. This is supported by Purohit and Benjwal who render Garh. tīg as ‘kamar – waist, loins’. The Garh. lemma derives possibly < PIE *(s)teigȗ- ‘flank, side’ with semantically quite close Russian stegnò ‘hip’ (see Matasović [2009: 387] and IEW: 1018).
